sections.h: The Korah psalms of Book II (Psalms 42–49)
sections.b: Book II of the Psalter opens with seven psalms whose titles name the sons of Korah: 42 and 44 to 49, with the untitled 43 belonging to 42. They include some of the best-loved songs of the Bible: the thirsting deer of Psalm 42, the royal wedding song of Psalm 45, "God is a shelter and strength for us" (Psalm 46), the enthronement hymn of Psalm 47, the Zion song of Psalm 48 and the wisdom poem on death and wealth of Psalm 49. Their recurring themes are the temple and Zion, longing for God's presence and God's kingship over the nations. Michael Goulder argued that the collection came from the northern sanctuary at Dan, near the Jordan's sources (Psalm 42:6); most scholars place the guild in Jerusalem, where Chronicles shows Korahites as gatekeepers and singers. It is a striking twist that the descendants of a rebel swallowed alive by Sheol (Numbers 16:33) sang that God would ransom their lives from Sheol's hand (Psalm 49:15).

uncommon: Goulder held that the Korah psalms were first sung at the autumn festival at Dan, and only later adapted for Jerusalem.

sections.b: The shift from "the LORD" to "God" begins abruptly with Psalm 42. In Psalms 42–43 the name YHWH occurs once (42:8); in Psalm 44 not at all; in Psalm 46 only in the refrain ("the LORD of Armies is with us") and in 46:8; in Psalm 47 twice; in Psalm 48 twice; in Psalms 49–53 almost never, except in the opening triple name of Psalm 50:1. Psalm 54:6 and Psalm 55:16 and 55:22 use the name once or twice each. Phrases such as "O God, my God" (Psalm 43:4) and "God, your God" (Psalm 45:7; Psalm 50:7) read like replacements for "O LORD my God" and "the LORD your God." The best evidence is Psalm 53, a second copy of Psalm 14 with "God" for "the LORD."

sections.h: Laments of Book II: absence, defeat, betrayal
sections.b: Book II opens with three different kinds of lament. Psalms 42–43 is the lament of one worshiper far from the temple, whose refrain argues with his own despair ("Why are you so bowed down, my soul? ... Wait for God"). Psalm 44 is a lament of the whole nation after defeat, which refuses to call its suffering punishment and ends by telling God to wake up. Psalm 55 is the lament of a person betrayed by a close friend in a violent city, who wishes for a dove's wings. Together they show the range of biblical complaint: honest about God's apparent absence, willing to protest, and still addressed to God.

common: Lament psalms usually move from complaint to trust, but Psalm 44 ends still pleading.

sections.b: Psalm 44 is one of the clearest Old Testament statements that God's people can suffer without having sinned. The nation recalls God's victories (Psalm 44:1–8), describes its defeat and scattering (Psalm 44:9–16), and swears that it has not forgotten God or broken the covenant (Psalm 44:17–21). Its conclusion is not an explanation but a cry: "No, it is on your account that we are killed all day long." Paul quotes that line in Romans 8:36 and answers it with the love of God in Christ, from which no suffering can separate believers (Romans 8:35–39).

sections.h: "For your sake we are killed all day long"
sections.b: Psalm 44:22 became a text for martyrs in both Judaism and Christianity. The Talmud applies it to a mother and her seven sons who died rather than bow to an idol (Bavli Gittin 57b), a story also told in 2 Maccabees 7, and the verse became a key text for kiddush hashem, dying for the sanctification of God's name. Paul quotes it in Romans 8:36 of believers persecuted for Christ.

sections.h: Psalm 45: the king addressed as God
sections.b: Psalm 45 was written for a royal wedding, but the Targum already calls its king "King Messiah," and Hebrews 1:8–9 quotes its sixth and seventh verses of the Son: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever... God, your God, has anointed you." The Hebrew line can be read as an address to the king as "God" (the most natural grammar) or as "your throne is God's." Jewish interpreters read the king as human, the Messiah or the righteous scholar; Christians see the Son, both addressed as God and anointed by God. The word "anointed" (mashach) in Psalm 45:7 is the root of "messiah."

Among the seven texts Hebrews 1:5–13 uses to show the Son's superiority to the angels is Psalm 45:6–7, read as God's words to the Son: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever." Most commentators take "O God" as an address to the Son, so that Hebrews calls him God while also saying God anointed him.

sections.h: The queen at the king's right hand (Psalm 45)
sections.b: Catholic and Orthodox liturgy apply Psalm 45:9–15 to Mary: the queen standing at the king's right hand in gold of Ophir, the daughter told to listen and forget her father's house, the king's daughter all glorious, led to the king with her companions. Pius XII listed these verses among the texts theologians used for her Assumption (Munificentissimus Deus 26), and Orthodox feasts of the Theotokos sing Greek Psalm 44:11 and 44:18 (English 45:10 and 45:17). Protestant interpreters read the queen and bride as the church.

Psalm 45 is the only wedding song in the Psalter. It praises the groom, a king, and gives advice to the bride, a foreign princess: "Forget your own people and your father's household." It shows a real royal marriage of alliance (compare 1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 16:31), and it became a key text for reading marriage as a picture of God and his people, alongside the Song of Songs and Ephesians 5.

sections.h: God as King of all the earth (Psalm 47)
sections.b: Psalm 47 calls every nation to clap and shout for God, "a great King over the whole earth," who "has gone up" with the ram's horn and taken his seat on his holy throne. With Psalms 93 and 95–99 it belongs to the "enthronement psalms." Mowinckel linked them with an autumn festival of God's kingship; Jews recite Psalm 47 on Rosh Hashanah, and Christians sing it on Ascension Day. Psalm 45, by contrast, praises the human king as God's anointed, whose throne is "for ever and ever."

Psalms 46 and 48 celebrate Zion as the city God protects. Psalm 46 gives it a river that gladdens it, though Jerusalem had no river, and a refrain of God's presence ("The LORD of Armies is with us"). Psalm 48 calls Mount Zion "the heights of Zaphon," claiming for Jerusalem the title of the Canaanite mountain of the gods, and tells of kings who saw the city and fled. Both psalms invite people to look: "Come, look at the LORD's deeds"; "Circle Zion, walk all around her." Jeremiah warned later against trusting the temple as a charm (Jeremiah 7:4), and Lamentations 2:15 quotes Psalm 48:2 over the ruined city.

sections.h: Psalms 49 and 52: no ransom from death
sections.b: Psalm 49 tells the poor not to fear the rich, because "No one can ever buy back a brother / or give God a ransom for him": the wise and the fool die alike and leave their wealth to others, and the rich man takes nothing with him. Psalm 52 mocks the "hero" who trusted in his great wealth instead of making God his stronghold. Jesus' parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21) and his question about gaining the world and losing one's life (Mark 8:36–37) carry the same teaching.

Psalm 49:14 pictures the self-confident herded into Sheol like sheep, with Death as their shepherd, a grim reversal of Psalm 23. Against that, the speaker trusts that God "will ransom my life / from the hand of Sheol" (Psalm 49:15). Psalm 55:15 prays that traitors "go down to Sheol alive," as Korah's band did (Numbers 16:33), and 55:23 speaks of "the well of the Pit."

Psalm 49:15 is one of the few Old Testament psalms that may hope for life with God beyond death. The verb "take" (laqach) is the one used of Enoch, whom God took (Genesis 5:24), and of Elijah (2 Kings 2:3), and it returns in Psalm 73:24. Some read the verse only as rescue from an early death; many Jewish and Christian interpreters read it as a hope that God will keep the faithful beyond the grave, a step toward the resurrection hope of Daniel 12:2.

sections.h: God does not need sacrifice (Psalms 50 and 51)
sections.b: Psalm 50 has God say that he will not take bulls or goats, because every animal is already his, and "Suppose I were hungry: I would not say so to you." What he wants is the thank offering, kept vows and a life that matches the covenant. Psalm 51 adds that no sacrifice could answer the speaker's sin: "A broken spirit: that is the sacrifice for God." Its last verse looks forward to sacrifices "offered rightly" again. After the temple fell in AD 70, the rabbis drew on these psalms to teach that prayer, repentance and thanks can take the place of offerings (Bavli Sanhedrin 43b; Leviticus Rabbah 9:7).
sections.refs: Psalm 50:8–15; Psalm 50:23; Psalm 51:16–19; 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Hebrews 13:15

sections.b: Psalm 51 is the Bible's fullest prayer of repentance. Its title places it after Nathan confronted David over Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12). It appeals to God's grace, loyal love and compassion (Exodus 34:6–7), names rebellion, guilt and sin, asks to be wiped, washed and purified with hyssop, and then asks for more than pardon: "Create a pure heart for me, O God, / and make a steady spirit new inside me." It has shaped Jewish and Christian penitence ever since: it is the fourth of the church's seven penitential psalms, the psalm of Ash Wednesday, and its 51:15 opens Jewish and Christian daily prayer.

common: Psalm 51 is the classic example of true repentance: honest confession, no excuses and trust in God's mercy.
uncommon: Some scholars think Psalm 51 was composed during the exile as Israel's confession, and only later linked with David.

sections.b: Psalm 51:5 became the Western church's chief Old Testament text for original sin, through Augustine and the Reformation confessions (the Formula of Concord; Westminster Confession 6.3). The Hebrew says the speaker was born in guilt and conceived in sin: a confession that his sinfulness goes back to the beginning of his life. Eastern Orthodox theology reads it of the fallen human condition, not of inherited guilt. Jewish interpreters read it of the evil inclination present from birth (Genesis 8:21), and a midrash has David say that his parents thought of their own pleasure, not of him (Leviticus Rabbah 14:5). The verse does not say that sex or conception is sinful.

Psalm 51:11 is one of only three places in the Hebrew Bible with the phrase "holy spirit" (the others are Isaiah 63:10–11). The speaker begs God not to take it from him, perhaps fearing the fate of Saul, from whom "the LORD's Spirit had turned away" (1 Samuel 16:14). Read in the Old Testament setting, it is God's holy presence and power with his servant; Christians read it of the Holy Spirit, and traditions differ on whether a believer can lose the Spirit.

sections.h: "Your holy spirit, do not take it from me"
sections.b: David's prayer in Psalm 51:11 is often cited in debates about whether believers can fall away. Reformed and many Baptist interpreters say the Spirit is never taken from the elect, and read the prayer as a plea for restored joy or for David's royal anointing. Catholic, Lutheran and Methodist teachers read it as evidence that grave sin can drive the Spirit away and that repentance restores him.

The title of Psalm 51 ties it to Nathan's rebuke of David "after David had come to Bathsheba," playing on the verb "come." The psalm never names Bathsheba or Uriah, but read with the title its "bloodguilt" (Psalm 51:14) is Uriah's death and its "against you alone" (Psalm 51:4) is David's acceptance of God's verdict (2 Samuel 12:9–13).

Psalm 55 laments a betrayal by "a man of my own rank, / my trusted friend," who once walked with the speaker to the house of God. Jewish and Christian tradition often identified this friend with Ahithophel, David's counselor who joined Absalom (2 Samuel 15:12, 31) and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). The Talmud says Ahithophel and Doeg died before half their days (Psalm 55:23; Bavli Sanhedrin 106b). Christians also heard Judas in the psalm.

sections.b: Two psalm titles in Book II recall betrayals during David's flight from Saul. Psalm 52 is set when Doeg the Edomite reported David's visit to the priest Ahimelech, which led to the massacre at Nob (1 Samuel 22:9–19). Psalm 54 is set when the Ziphites told Saul that David was hiding among them (1 Samuel 23:19; 1 Samuel 26:1).

Psalms 52–55 contain short prayers and announcements against enemies: God will pull down and uproot the liar (Psalm 52:5); "By your faithfulness, put an end to them" (Psalm 54:5); "let them go down to Sheol alive" (Psalm 55:15). They hand vengeance to God rather than taking it, and they follow real betrayals: a report that led to a massacre, a town that gave up a fugitive, a friend turned traitor. The Roman Liturgy of the Hours (1971) leaves out the harshest such verses in a number of psalms (General Instruction 131); other traditions pray them whole.
sections.refs: Psalm 52:5–7; Psalm 54:5; Psalm 55:9; Psalm 55:15; Psalm 55:23; Romans 12:19

sections.b: Book II's titles show the main types. Some name a collection ("of the sons of Korah," 42–49; "of Asaph," 50). Some give the music: "For the music director," "With stringed instruments" (54, 55), "On 'Lilies'" (45), "On alamoth" (46), "On mahalath" (53). Some name a kind of song (maskil, psalm, song, "a love song"). And three tie a psalm to an event in David's life: Nathan's rebuke (51), Doeg's report (52) and the Ziphites' betrayal (54). Psalm 43 has no title, a sign it belongs with 42. The Greek translators often guessed at the meanings: "for those who will be changed" (45), "concerning hidden things" (46).

sections.b: Several psalms of this section have had a long life in worship. Psalm 43 opened the Roman Mass for four centuries. Psalm 48 was the temple's Monday psalm (Mishnah Tamid 7:4) and still is in the synagogue. Psalm 47 is recited seven times before the shofar on Rosh Hashanah and sung on Ascension Day. Psalm 51:15, "Lord, open my lips," opens the Amidah and the Christian daily office. Luther's "A mighty fortress" paraphrases Psalm 46.

sections.h: Korah and Asaph in Book II
sections.b: Chronicles names three guilds of Levite singers: Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 25:1). Book II opens with psalms of the sons of Korah (Psalms 42–49) and of Asaph (Psalm 50). Heman's line descends from Korah (1 Chronicles 6:33–37), so the "sons of Korah" psalms may belong to the Heman guild; Heman is named in the title of Psalm 88, and Jeduthun appears in the titles of Psalms 39, 62 and 77.

sections.h: "God of gods, the LORD" and "God, your God"
sections.b: Psalm 50:1 opens with three names, El Elohim YHWH, as in Joshua 22:22. In the Elohistic Psalter, forms like "God, your God" (Psalm 50:7) stand where other books say "the LORD your God." Psalm 46:7 joins "the LORD of Armies" with "with us" ('immanu), the heart of Isaiah's name Immanuel.

In this section God's hesed is what the speakers lean on when everything else fails: the LORD "gives orders for his loyal love" by day (Psalm 42:8); a defeated nation asks to be ransomed "for your loyal love's sake" (Psalm 44:26); worshipers ponder it in the temple (Psalm 48:9); the boaster is reminded that it lasts all day (Psalm 52:1), and the faithful trust it "for ever and ever" (Psalm 52:8). Psalm 51:1 begins, "Be gracious to me, O God, as your loyal love is."
sections.refs: Psalm 42:8; Psalm 44:26; Psalm 48:9; Psalm 51:1; Psalm 52:1; Psalm 52:8; Exodus 34:6–7

sections.b: These psalms name the lyre (Psalm 43:4; Psalm 49:4), stringed instruments (Psalm 54:0; Psalm 55:0), the ram's horn (Psalm 47:5), tune names such as "Lilies" (Psalm 45:0), and possibly voice registers ("alamoth," Psalm 46:0). Psalm 49 even presents a wisdom teaching as a riddle opened "with the lyre."

sections.b: Psalm 55:17 ("At evening, at morning, at midday / I pour out my complaint") and Daniel 6:10 are often cited for the three daily times of Jewish prayer. Psalm 44:23 shows how boldly Israel could pray: "Get up! Why do you sleep, Lord?"
